mcqs.question: How does the answer to "how does your design cope with a launch flash crowd" differ from the answer to "scale to 10x traffic"?
options: It focuses on controlling how much load ever reaches the backend — edge-level shedding and gradual rollout — rather than just scaling backend capacity bigger
The two questions have identical correct answers, since both are about traffic growth
It focuses purely on choosing a bigger cloud instance type for the database
It's only about estimating the exact number of new users precisely in advance
mcqs.explanation: A flash crowd needs an architectural posture — admission control at the edge, gradual rollout — because backend capacity can't be conjured instantly, unlike steady growth where you have time to scale layer by layer. Precise user-count estimation and simply resizing the database don't address the sudden, uncontrolled nature of the surge.

mcqs.question: Why watch metrics at each step of a 1% -> 10% -> 100% gradual rollout, rather than moving straight to 100% once 1% looks fine?
options: Regulatory requirements mandate a fixed number of rollout stages
Capacity or correctness problems can appear only at higher traffic levels, so each step needs its own check before widening further
Rolling out gradually is required only for mobile apps, not web services
Metrics at 1% are always sufficient to predict behavior at 100%
mcqs.explanation: A problem that doesn't show up at 1% traffic can appear at 10% or 100% as load-dependent bottlenecks emerge, so each step needs its own verification rather than extrapolating from the first. There's no such regulatory or platform-specific requirement driving this.

mcqs.question: Why must the waiting room admitting users into a system be extremely cheap and horizontally scalable itself?
options: Cheap components are inherently more secure than expensive ones
It's a stylistic preference with no functional impact on the system's resilience
The waiting room now absorbs the entire uncontrolled surge, so if it does real per-request work, the bottleneck just moves one hop earlier instead of being solved
Waiting rooms are legally required to have minimal per-request cost
mcqs.explanation: The waiting room becomes the new front line for the entire surge, so any real per-request work it does (like a database lookup) recreates the same overload problem one layer earlier — it has to be near-free to actually protect anything behind it. This isn't about security or legal requirements, and it clearly does affect resilience, not just style.

mcqs.question: A team relies purely on autoscaling to handle a launch flash crowd, with no edge-level admission control. What's the risk?
options: There is no risk — autoscaling reacts instantly to any traffic increase
Autoscaling only works for database tiers, never for application servers
The risk is purely financial, from paying for unnecessary extra capacity
New capacity takes time to boot and warm up, and a sudden flash crowd can overwhelm existing capacity in seconds, well before autoscaling catches up
mcqs.explanation: Autoscaling has a real reaction delay — new instances need to boot, warm up, and join the pool — while a flash crowd can flood existing capacity in seconds. Autoscaling applies to app servers as much as (often more than) database tiers, and the risk here is availability, not primarily cost.
